item.title: SpaceX no longer needs NASA, and that’s a problem for America’s space agency
item.description:
“NASA desperately needs SpaceX, and SpaceX knows it, and Elon knows it.”

For nearly a quarter of a century, Elon Musk and his essential partner at SpaceX, Gwynne Shotwell, viewed the United States government as El Dorado, the mythical city of gold.

Like machete-wielding treasure hunters, Musk and Shotwell hacked through a tangled jungle filled with lurking carnivores such as Boeing and Lockheed Martin, as well as bean counters and regulators. Over time, against long odds, the pair cleared a path for SpaceX to contracts at NASA and the US military. They sued when things did not go their way. They hollered about unfair playing fields. Most importantly, they delivered quality space products to the US government for less.

And so, after a while, SpaceX found El Dorado and a city of contracts.

Then they started winning everything. So much so that the relationship between the customer and contractor began to change. Slowly at first, but ever more quickly, SpaceX went from needing the US government as an indispensable customer to becoming an indispensable contractor for the nation.

The pendulum has swung so far now that SpaceX seems increasingly disinterested in the US government for most contracts outside of data services, such as Starshield for military communications and observations.

“I guess I am still in denial that there is a divorce pending,” said Lori Garver, a deputy NASA administrator during the Obama White House years who was instrumental in expanding the agency’s use of commercial contracts with companies like SpaceX. “I literally cannot wrap my head around a future yet where SpaceX stops flying Dragon and Falcon. Not yet.”

But the signs point to at least a partial breakup. Consider the following data points:

To be clear, SpaceX is still fulfilling its existing contracts with NASA, the US Space Force, and other government entities. And it continues to do so at a lower cost and generally higher level of reliability than pretty much anyone else.

But the company is no longer signing many large new contracts for spaceflight services, at least in the traditional launch and in-space flight domains. The shift comes after 15 years in which the US government has grown accustomed to lower costs and rapid innovation that has revitalized the nation’s access to space.

For SpaceX and its shareholders, as shocking as it may seem for a US company to leave billions of dollars on the table in government contracts, this may be the right decision. SpaceX sees the vast bulk of its future revenue coming from artificial intelligence. However, SpaceX’s retreat from the public square comes as both NASA and the Space Force confront growing challenges from a rising space program in China and an aging but still dangerous Russia in space.

So what does it mean if the halcyon days of SpaceX riding to the rescue for America in space—such as in the saga of Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams—seem to be ending?

In the early days, Musk and Shotwell sought revenue from various sources as SpaceX developed the scrappy Falcon 1 rocket. But it was NASA that stepped in at two crucial moments in the company’s first decade.

The first came in 2006, with a $278 million award to develop a cargo delivery spacecraft for the International Space Station. It helped SpaceX expand rapidly when it was struggling to develop the Falcon 1 rocket. An even more consequential award arrived in December 2008, $1.6 billion for a dozen Dragon cargo flights to the space station. The funding arrived as SpaceX struggled to meet payroll. Both Musk and Shotwell have said this award probably saved SpaceX from bankruptcy.

NASA and SpaceX then fell into an increasingly warm and mutually beneficial relationship. During the last two decades, NASA has awarded contracts to SpaceX worth approximately $20 billion, and Musk has been deeply appreciative. In 2017,he revealedthat the online password for some of his accounts was “ILoveNASA.” In return, NASA got reliable cargo, eventually crew services into low-Earth orbit, and a revolution in US spaceflight capabilities.

Musk and Shotwell fought to extend their relationship with the federal government in the mid-2010s. In 2014, they filed a lawsuit against the US Air Force for the right to bid for national security launch contracts. Musk contended that United Launch Alliance had a monopoly and said SpaceX should be eligible to bid. “We’re just protesting and saying these launches should be competed,”he saidat the time. “And if we compete and lose, that’s fine, but why were they not even competed?”

The effort proved successful. SpaceX won national security contracts, and launch costs for the military plunged. Over time, SpaceX became the dominant player. Even today, with United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin struggling to bring their large Vulcan and New Glenn rockets into service, SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets have become a single-point failure for national security launches. If the US military needed to get a dozen large satellites into orbit during the next 12 to 18 months, there is only one company that could credibly pull that off.

The bottom line is that SpaceX, far more often than any other competitor over the last 15 years, delivered spaceflight services to the US government when other contractors were late or overbudget or simply failed. That no other commercial space company has risen alongside SpaceX during this period is a problem. NASA, certainly, sought to support competitors such as Blue Origin, Sierra Space, Rocket Lab, Orbital Sciences, Boeing, and others. The US military supported development of United Launch Alliance’s rocket with $2 billion in funding as an alternative to Falcon.

And still, none have yet come remotely close to matching what SpaceX has done in launch, spacecraft, and in-space data services.

The relationship dynamic began to change about half a decade ago.

At the height of the pandemic, in mid-2020, SpaceX delivered a huge win for NASA by safely flying astronauts Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken to the space station. It is difficult to overstate the importance of this achievement for NASA. Since 2011, the space agency had swallowed its pride and gone, hat in hand, to Russia for transportation to the space station. Its astronauts spent months in Russia learning the language and training to ride the Soyuz spacecraft into orbit. With a single successful 64-day mission, SpaceX ended all of that.

Less than a year later, NASA again turned to SpaceX. The space agency needed a Moon lander. But Congress had only appropriated beer money for a champagne project. NASA had three options for a privately developed lunar lander. None were ideal. SpaceX’s $2.89 billion proposal to develop Starship as a lunar lander and fly two missions was the only bid that fit NASA’s budget profile. Yes, Starship presented a complicated, oversized, and technically demanding solution. But in 2021, SpaceX was NASA’s only spaceflight contractor consistently delivering big results.

Almost overnight, then, NASA’s two most important and costly programs, the Artemis Program to land humans on the Moon and the International Space Station, became utterly dependent on SpaceX.

This power imbalance continued to grow, breaking into wider public view in June 2025 amid a temporary falling out between Musk and the president he helped elect. After Trump threatened to “terminate” SpaceX’s governmental contracts and subsidies, Musk’s response was essentiallyso what? In return,Musk threatenedto decommission the Dragon spacecraft. He knew—correctly, it turns out—that SpaceX’s role in US government space programs could not be easily replaced.A Pentagon reviewin July 2025 found most of the company’s contracts with the US Department of Defense were essential.

Trump could still have hurt Musk’s businesses through regulatory review, particularly with the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Aviation Administration. And the two made up. But one indisputable takeaway from this brouhaha is that the US government now needed SpaceX more than SpaceX needed the US government.

“The dust-up with President Trump, when Musk threatened to take away Dragon, was utterly irresponsible,” said Chris Davenport, a professor at Arizona State University and author ofRocket Dreams. “If Falcon and Dragon go away, that is a huge disservice to the US government. NASA desperately needs SpaceX, and SpaceX knows it, and Elon knows it.”

This represented a truly remarkable shift for everyone who watched SpaceX fight so hard, for so long, to get its foot in the door at NASA and the Space Force. But as jarring as it is, this shift is no longer deniable.

Around the time of his dispute with Trump, Musk came to fully believe that artificial intelligence was not just the next big thing. Rather, it wastheindustrial revolution of his lifetime. He began vectoring his two biggest companies, Tesla and SpaceX, toward dominating AI software, AI hardware, and computing power on the ground and in space to run it all.

This largely explains SpaceX’s acquisition of xAI and its subsequent IPO. It is also behind the potential merger of SpaceX and Tesla. This will give Musk more direct control over Tesla, something he values. But more critically, it gives him an immense pool of assets to deploy toward building data centers terrestrially and in space, autonomous vehicles, robots, massive rockets, and more.

No other company on Earth has the potential, at least in the near term, to own an entire stack of artificial intelligence. Elon Musk wants to manufacture the chips and electricity infrastructure for data centers, he wants to build the data centers that will power the AI revolution, he wants to develop and train the AI models that will provide its intelligence, and he wants to build physical products that he believes will become the shaping force of the 21st century.

He wants it all.

Such a future, in his mind, does not include a dead-end technology like the Dragon spacecraft—even though Dragon is the only reliable way to get humans into space outside of China and Russia, and only took flight with humans six years ago. He does not want to fly the partially reusable Falcon 9 rocket—even though it is the best, cheapest, and only Western vehicle capable of expanding to meet the growing demand from government and commercial customers for access to space right now.

Musk believes the government moves too slowly and simply isn’t ambitious enough when it comes to space. Often, in meetings at SpaceX, he will describe working with the US government as “like wearing lead shoes and walking through molasses.”

Instead, Musk wants to build bigger things, like Starship. He wants to move fast and break things when necessary. This explains why he has invested something like $15 billion in the development of the Starship rocket, from its engines to a growing number of launch sites in Texas and Florida, to get the massive, fully reusable vehicle off the ground.

For a time, this looked like a win-win situation for the US government and a growing commercial space industry counting on frequent, low-cost access to space. NASA built its Artemis Program around Starships landing on the Moon. The commercial space industry looked forward to abundant, cheap launches. The general sense was that pulling Dragon and Falcon 9 off the market would cause temporary upheaval, but these problems would soon be ameliorated by Starship and its promise of lower cost and even greater capability.

That was the hope, at least.

In March 2020, SpaceXpublished its first“Starship Users Guide,” which included a 9-meter payload fairing with a “clamshell” structure that would open once in space to deploy payloads. The company said it would support Falcon-compatible payload adapters.

But in recent years, there has been little evidence that SpaceX is actually developing such a deployment mechanism. Rather, the company has implemented a Pez-like dispenser that releases flattish satellites from a narrow door in the middle of the Starship vehicle. This serves SpaceX’s internal payloads of Starlink and future Starmind (data center) satellites. But it’s unsuitable for deploying more traditional satellites or big NASA payloads, such as large space telescopes.

Multiple people Ars spoke with for this story said it would be incredibly beneficial if SpaceX publicly committed to developing a large payload door and provided a timeline for its readiness. Ars offered SpaceX the opportunity to make such a commitment, but the company didn’t take it.

And it doesn’t have to. The reality is straightforward. This year’s IPO gave SpaceX a laser-like focus on its core business plan. Reaching stratospheric financial targets requires launching incredible numbers of Starlink and Starmind satellites, all of which can be dispensed like Pez candy into space. Launch services for third parties, which include NASA and other Moon Base customers, represent a rounding error in SpaceX’s revenue in the post-IPO world.

In its recent third-quarter10-Q financial filing, the company references these launch priorities for Starlink and artificial intelligence: “We allocate a significant amount of launch capacity to our Connectivity segment and expect to allocate a significant amount to our SI segment in the future.”

An argument often made about SpaceX’s decision to end the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rocket is that these programs—which operate with unprecedented efficiency in the history of launch—consume valuable engineering time. This talented team pushed Falcon 9 above 150 launches a year and helped make SpaceX globally dominant. Musk has said he would like to redirect these talented engineers to bring similar launch-operation efficiency to the Starship program.

Great engineers are certainly a finite resource. And SpaceX faces fierce competition in the US space industry for talented engineers, with higher salaries offered by Blue Origin, and attractive alternatives such as Stoke Space, Rocket Lab, Firefly, and Relativity Space all recruiting.

The question is whether Musk would devote his Falcon engineering team solely to Starship. Perhaps not. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call in October, Musk made a striking comment while musing about how the company aimed to deploy 10 GW of compute (on Earth) in 2027.

“What we’ve done at SpaceX is we’ve taken a team that has been able to achieve a market share in mass to orbit that is almost 90 percent,” Musk said. That team, he added, “has been able to achieve results that are an order of magnitude greater than the rest of all competitors in space combined.” Now, he said, SpaceX was applying that same team to the deployment of terrestrial compute. They would not be sent to Starbase for Starship, in other words, but to places like Memphis, Tennessee.

“This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League,” Musk said. “It’s not fair. But the net result is being able to deploy power, cooling, and infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than anyone else and may at some point be faster than everyone else combined.”

So yeah.

SpaceX can do what it wants. But there are consequences, and some people at NASA are starting to wonder how serious SpaceX is about the Human Landing System contract it won from NASA in 2021. Landing on the Moon is wholly tangential to the company’s near-term AI future, and fulfilling the contract will almost certainly be a net negative from a financial perspective.

SpaceX, of course, says it is working assiduously on a lunar lander. And publicly, NASA officials say the company is a good partner. In an interview with Ars last week, the manager of the Artemis Program for NASA, Jeremy Parsons, said he regularly visits SpaceX facilities in Hawthorne, California, and Starbase, Texas. “Their management team is definitely committed to the lunar missions,” he said. Parsons credited the SpaceX engineers working on Starship as “some of the smartest individuals” he had ever met.

No one I have spoken to at NASA, both on and off the record, says SpaceX has given them a reason to believe the company will not eventually meet its Human Landing System commitments. And to date, SpaceX has had a remarkably good track record of delivering for NASA on its contracts. Nevertheless, the road ahead may be rocky in an era when SpaceX is pulling back from government involvement.

SpaceX has consistently told NASA it must get Starship flying orbital missions regularly. It has to get to full reusability, or nothing else matters. It has to do propellant transfer. All of that must come before finalizing the lander. And sure, it’s totally fair to say that the most important thing SpaceX can do for NASA right now is getting Starship to a very high flight rate. In SpaceX’s view, in a few years, Starship will be flying so often—the companyrecently toldthe Federal Aviation Administration it plans to launch 10,000 Starships a year by the 2030s—that fueling depots for missions to the Moon and Mars will be trivial.

Such a launch cadence surely would change everything, but nothing in aerospace ever happens as fast as one thinks or wants. And for now, the real issue is just how committed SpaceX is to the lander project and NASA’s competition with China. At SpaceX, projects deemed most important by leadership get the most resources. That is, the best engineers, the most software support, the most funding, and so on. Those projects are currently things like Starmind, theColossus data centerproject in Memphis, and Starship engineering. It’s not the Human Landing System, multiple sources told Ars.

As SpaceX has struggled through the Starship test flight program, NASA has been waiting for an in-space fueling test, which has slipped its schedule many times. Testing propellant transfer and storage at a large scale is critical, and it has never been done in space. Successfully completing this test would reduce much of the risk for the kinds of refueling operations needed to send a fully loaded Starship to the Moon.

The latest target for such a test is “early” 2027, according to NASA and SpaceX. But this date seems aspirational. According to Parsons, the test requires one Starship to launch from Starbase in Texas and another to launch from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Starship has not yet flown from there. Presently, a debut Florida launch is not expected until at least January. According to Parsons, the in-orbit fueling test is the third launch planned from Florida.

Once SpaceX demonstrates in-orbit refueling, it could begin planning a campaign to send an uncrewed Starship to land on the Moon as a demonstration. How many tanker launches would this take? The internal estimate at NASA’s Johnson Space Center is “about 22” Starship launches,Ars reported last week.Musk followed that upby saying the actual number “will be more like 6 to 8.”

So what’s the truth? In the near term, given Starship’s lift capacity, a lunar landing will probably require about 20 launches, which is the most current publicly disclosed government planning figure. With improvements to Starship andRaptor engine performance, and as SpaceX gets a better handle on in-space refueling operations, that number will assuredly come down. So at some point in the future, it could be as low as six. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman appeared to confirm this last week when he characterized Musk’s estimate of six to eight refueling flights as the “ultimate potential end state” of Starship.

Unfortunately, to beat China back to the Moon by 2030, NASA can’t wait for Starship to reach its final form. If SpaceX were to fly a lunar demonstration in the next year or two, a necessary precursor to human landings, it probably would take something like 20 Starship launches. Starship has flown 14 times in the last three and a half years. Its flight ratewill undoubtedly acceleratein the coming months, but even at a weekly launch cadence, fueling a Starship for a lunar landing would still require more than four months of dedicated launches.

Frankly, it’s difficult to envision SpaceX dedicating 20 Starships to a NASA mission anytime soon. The opportunity cost is enormous. Those same rockets could launch hundreds of revenue-generating Starlink V3 satellites into orbit. A single Starlink launch on Starship delivers the same amount of bandwidth as 10 Falcon 9 launches—bandwidth SpaceX can sell to customers for years to come. And as SpaceX expands into artificial intelligence, the company has even greater incentives to reserve Starship’s capacity for its own growing constellation of satellites.

And then there’s the financial burden. Let’s assume an unoptimized launch cost of $100 million for early Starship flights—still a phenomenally low number for a super heavy lift vehicle. At that price, a lunar landing campaign requiring 20 launches would cost approximately $2 billion in launch expenses alone. Recall that SpaceX’s original Human Landing System contract was valued at $2.89 billion and included both an uncrewed demo and crewed landing.

The actual cost of a single lunar landing mission remains uncertain, and some of the investments needed to fulfill the contract will benefit Starship more broadly. But the larger point is clear: NASA is asking SpaceX to devote substantial resources to a program that offers comparatively little financial upside at a time when the company’s own commercial ambitions are growing exponentially.

Imagine a world where SpaceX had goneall inon developing a lunar lander. Would the company be taking a different approach to the immense technical challenges of getting Starship to the Moon, perhaps with a stubby Starship variant? Would it be devoting more of its best engineers to the program? Would it consider using an expendable tanker Starship to reduce the total needed?

SpaceX very well might still get to the Moon in the next five years, and the company has enormous technical capacity. Its history suggests that when Musk makes something an overriding priority, things happen quickly. All it would take for SpaceX to go full throttle on a lunar Starship would be for Musk to text a technical leader at the company something like, “Do HLS.”

Last year, Ars asked Musk if it mattered to him that China gets back to the Moon before NASA with the Artemis Program.

“I think the United States should be aiming for Mars, because we’ve already actually been to the Moon several times,”he replied. “Yeah, if China sort of equals that, I’m like, OK, sure, but that’s something that America did 56 years ago.”

In November of last year, Ars posed a similar question to Blue Origin’s chief executive, Dave Limp. “We just want to help the US get to the Moon,”he said. “If NASA wants to go quicker, we would move heaven and Earth, pun intended, to try to get to the Moon sooner.”

Multiple NASA sources said Blue really is doing whatever it takes to help NASA and that what once appeared as a rocky relationship is now flourishing.

After SpaceX won a sole-source contract for the Human Landing System in 2021, Blue Origin sued NASA. This pressure, along with NASA’s desire for a second provider, led Congress to eventually add funding for a second lander. As with Starship, Blue Origin’s original design under this new contractalso involved refueling operationsin low-Earth orbit for the large Blue Moon Mark 2 vehicle.

As it became increasingly clear that China was on course to land humans on the Moon by or before 2030, Blue Origin’s large and ambitious Blue Moon lander did not serve NASA’s more immediate needs. It would take too long.

In 2025,Ars was first to reportthat Blue Origin might be able to develop a lunar landing system that involved a smaller version of the Blue Moon Mark 2 vehicle and multiple transfer stages based on the existing Mark 1 lander. This involved a significant redesign to the Blue Moon program, but critically, it removed the need for in-space refueling. Eventually, this became the new plan. Blue Origin, without any guarantee of new funding, changed its design when NASA needed something faster.

“I will tell you, they are absolutely fantastic partners,” Parsons, NASA’s Artemis manager, said of Blue Origin. “They have leaned forward at every step, and they are all in on the mission.”

NASA’s upcoming Artemis III mission is illustrative of the differences.

The mission is intended to test both Blue Origin and SpaceX’s lunar landers in space. Blue Origin is building a special “test” version of its Blue Moon lander to demonstrate a host of capabilities for NASA. After docking, the crew will exit the Orion spacecraft and spend time aboard the Blue Moon vehicle. By contrast, SpaceX is pulling a “ship off the line” of its Starship program for the flight. Orion will rendezvous and dock with Starship, but there will be no ingress into the vehicle and hence no life support equipment.

Earlier this year, NASA revealeda major new initiativeto develop a Moon Base. Not long after, New Glenn exploded on its launch pad. In the aftermath, Blue Origin has moved with uncharacteristic speed to repair its launch pad to get New Glenn flying again, whileinvesting $3 billionin Florida facilities to support a much higher launch cadence.

This matters because New Glenn is superseding Starship as the essential rocket powering NASA’s lunar ambitions.

Beyond the Human Landing System, there are myriad robotic elements of the Moon Base that need to get to the surface, and NASA has contracted with a host of US space companies to develop smaller cargo landers.Some of these providersare growing nervous about launch. At least two of these companies had “rough order of magnitude” estimates and other types of launch agreements with SpaceX for Falcon 9s to deliver elements of NASA’s Moon base later this decade. But in the last several weeks, SpaceX, the only company that can offer reliable launch dates, has told them it will no longer sell rides to the Moon.

This has sent shockwaves through the Artemis community. It is not the behavior of a partner being broadly supportive of NASA’s lunar efforts. These smaller lander companies now must hope that New Glenn can pick up the slack or a company like Relativity Space can bring its Terran R rocket to readiness quickly.

Ars pressed Parsons on how committed SpaceX really was to NASA’s lunar activities. For example, did he really believe SpaceX would be willing to sideline its profitable Starlink and Starmind launches for the extended period to support an Artemis landing? “It’s a fair question, especially as they have gone public,” he acknowledged.

For more than a decade, NASA more or less turned its spaceflight fortunes over to one billionaire. That partnership now appears to be unraveling, and there seems to be a growing sense that if the space agency is to achieve its considerable lunar ambitions in the next decade, it may need another billionaire to bail it out.

“This could end up being a very big opportunity for Blue Origin and Jeff Bezos, who would absolutely relish the role of coming to the country in its time of need,” said Davenport, the author who has written about the rocket billionaires. “Bezos has been public in saying he wanted to serve his country, particularly if it meant in doing it instead of SpaceX and Elon.”

Bezos, of course, is not doing this out of the goodness of his heart or because he bleeds red, white, and blue. He stands to gain Artemis customers, national security launch contracts, and commercial business. He is chasing SpaceX’s enormous valuation with his own space company. But no one thinks Bezos would pull his rockets off the market if NASA were desperate to get to the Moon.

The real question is whether Blue Origin can succeed. The company has a long, long list of things to achieve to make Artemis a reality, from rockets to landers to in-space operations. And for all the many billions of dollars Bezos has invested, Blue Origin has a short track record of execution. It has only ever launched three orbital missions.

Now it is being called on to spearhead the landing of humans on the Moon. On a rocket that recently blew up. Aboard a lander that doesn’t yet exist. At the 11th hour.

item.title: Massive leak exposes 41,000 DHS workers and undercover ICE agents
item.description:
The leak reveals undercover agents, surveillance groups, and sensitive DHS access.

An unprecedented leak ofDepartment of Homeland Securityrecords has exposed details of more than 41,000 employees or contractors who work for the department and its constituent agencies. The records include email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses, but also references to internal systems and sensitive information on undercover and surveillance programs. In all, the leak provides a map of howDHSis organized and how it operates.

The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofitDistributed Denial of Secretsand cybersecurity researcher and journalistmaia arson crimewpreviewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace.

DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls “Icepick,” on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS’s Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.”

An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. “We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” the spokesperson says.

The leak comes as DHS has aggressivelypursued its critics, seeking tounmaskanonymous social media users, obtaincustomer recordson protesters, andsecure warrantsfor surveillance tools aimed at reporters. Since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS and the federal government have moved to hide DHS employees’names and faces. The agency has alsoexpanded its definitionof “doxing”—a term that typically refers to publishing someone’s home address and other personal details for malicious purposes—to encompass the publication of basic facts about public employees, like their names and titles.

The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. Law enforcement agencies have arrested several suspects and detained another who is alleged to be part of the group.

The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don’t think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED.

“DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.”

The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. The FBI referred WIRED’s inquiry to DHS.

According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors.

Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI’s St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references “Keyhole,” which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’sundercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groupsearlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).”

The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media.

Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS’s web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who hasreturned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment

Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer.

“If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.”

More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencingSignal, the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencingMobile Fortify, a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. About half are in Texas, California, and Arizona.

Roughly 1,300 ICE enforcement accounts have been created since July 4, 2025, when Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which funded the hiring of 10,000 new ICE Enforcement and Removal officers by the end of 2025.

Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members.

Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnelauthorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties. Many listcounty sheriff’s officesand jails as their workplaces. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.”

More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department.

The Trump administration hasprosecuted protestersfor posting information about individual ICE officers andwarned othersfor doing so. In June, 15 Minnesota residents were charged under laws related to stalking and threats of violence, which prosecutors linked to their participation in ICE-opposition activities.More than 100 HSI agents, including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats.

Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the nonprofit civil liberties group FIRE, says that the Trump administration has taken an expansive view of18 USC 119, a law that prohibits people from sharing “restricted personal information” about federal officers or their families with the intent to threaten them.

“This is information that would be on a business card,” says Steinbaugh of the names and basic work details included in the archive. “That’s not something the government can criminalize.”

Despite the potential sensitivity of other records in the leaked data, the creators of Icepick do not consider it doxing. They see it as an accountability tool.

“The DHS especially as an agency completely lacks accountability, despite many parts of it being incredibly unpopular. The people who work there know this too; for example, some of their LinkedIn bios simply say ‘stuff at US Government,’” says crimew. “If they weren’t hiding their involvement in the repressive arm of the US government, there would be no need for us to expose them in the first place.”

This story originally appeared onwired.com.

item.title: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it’s fixing that with more ads
item.description:
Google’s negative cash flow balloons to -$9.06 billion, and stock price tumbles following Q3 earnings.

Google parent Alphabetreported its Q3 financial resultson Wednesday afternoon, showing a healthy rise in revenue for the months of July to September. But the company’s stock price has taken a beating, marking one of the largest post-earnings drops in its history. It comes down to several troubling aspects of the new report, including an admission by the company that AI search isn’t earning as much as organic search, and despite that, Google expects to spend even more on AI next year.

The company took in almost $128 billion in Q3 2026, earning more than $26 billion in net income. These may sound like good numbers, but financial markets are not impressed. While revenue is up 25 percent versus last year, net income is almost $9 billion lower. As of this story’s publication, the stock price is down almost 12 percent, and it was down about 13 percent earlier in the day.

While revenue was up 25 percent year over year, analysts expected more. Google reported earnings per share of $2.12, but the consensus projection ahead of Wednesday was $3.02. Google’s Cloud products actually beat expectations, crossing $30 billion in revenue. That’s about a billion more than analyst guesses.

Google is still making a huge amount of money, but there are several troubling trends emerging. The last few years at the company have been all about AI, with generative technology appearing in products from Gmail to Android. Most notably, Google isshifting to an AI search platformpowered by Gemini models.

During the earnings call, Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindlerdiscussedthe company’s search volume. This is one of the key metrics by which Google tracks its own performance. In the last quarter, Google saw search grow by 12 percent versus last year. Good for the company, right? Except that’s a much slower rate than previous quarters. Growth in Q2 was 17 percent, and Q1 saw 19 percent growth over 2025. Search revenue was also flat in Q3.

So that’s the first problem, likely driven by more consumers using AI chatbots to find answers. The other issue is that Google’s take on AI search isn’t pulling in revenue like standard web search yet. According to Schindler, each AI Mode query earns less revenue compared to a similar web search—there are fewer ads, and they cost less to run.

While Schindler suggested AI mode revenue was set to increase, he was also careful to control expectations. Advertisers may need time, he said, to understand the value in AI search ads. The company’s research reportedly shows that users find these ads more relevant and helpful than the ones they see in traditional search.

As part of the financial disclosure, Google announced an expansion of ads in AI Mode. If you do decide to dip into Google’s search chatbot, you’ll probably see more contextual advertising. These ads will begin appearing in more international markets soon. In the US, where AI Mode ads were already becoming commonplace, Google will implement multi-turn ads. That means the sponsored links will change continuously as you engage in a back-and-forth with the robot. CEO Sundar Pichai noted that these complex interactions are becoming more common as Google pushes more users toward AI Mode.

Google is not slowing down—it’s only going to accelerate the shift toward more AI. Likelast quarter, Google reported negative cash flow in Q3. The loss actually increased from -$5.8 billion to -$9.06 billion, a situation that is directly attributable to Google’s runaway AI spending. Google had capital expenditures of $51.4 billion in Q3 and says it still expects total 2026 spending to be between $195 billion and $205 billion. In 2027, Google is targeting more than $300 billion of AI investment.

To support this continued spending, Google points to its cloud revenue more than doubling over the past year. It’s easy to see why the company is so keen to keep expanding in AI based on that. The company’s AI compute infrastructure doesn’t just power Gemini. Countless AI startups pay to run models on Google’s infrastructure. But even the larger AI firms are using venture cash to do it, and if that funding were to dry up, Google’s cloud revenues could go with it.

While Google’s investments ensure it still turns a profit, the trend of spending more than it earns on products and services (that negative cash flow) could come back to bite it. Search growth is declining, and Google is placing all its eggs in the AI basket. If spending on cloud services in the industry drops or search growth stalls, the company could be looking at a lot more red in its future.

item.title: Trump admin sues Utah to save Kalshi from the state’s total ban on gambling
item.description:
US agency has sued 10 states for trying to stop gambling on prediction markets.

The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets.

Utah, which prohibits gambling,sued Kalshiin a state court last week. Utah’s lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events.

“Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”

Utah already defeated Kalshi in federal court after the prediction market filed a preemptive lawsuit that sought to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling laws. Now that Utah is moving ahead in its attempt to shut down Kalshi, it must defend against alawsuitfiled by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

The CFTC “has filed a lawsuit against Utah to block the state’s efforts to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets using state laws,” thecommission said yesterday. “The lawsuit follows Utah’s decision to file civil enforcement actions in state court against CFTC-regulated markets and other businesses. Utah’s effort to restrict the functioning of CFTC-registered exchanges obstructs Congress’s decision to federally preempt state law.”

If Utah can shut down Kalshi, that could spell trouble for Kalshi’s chief prediction-market rival, Polymarket, and for sports betting sites like DraftKings and FanDuel. DraftKings and FanDuel advertiseavailability in all US statesvia amix of products, including prediction-market platforms in states like Utah. Both are registered with the CFTC.

The Utah attorney general’s office declined to comment today on the CFTC lawsuit. The CFTC previously filedlawsuitsagainst Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Kentucky, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin. The federal agency also filed briefs supporting Kalshi in appeals court cases.

“Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets,” CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said. “Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes—they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets. As I’ve said before, the CFTC has the expertise and responsibility to defend its exclusive jurisdiction over commodity derivatives, and that’s exactly what we’ll do.”

The US Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) gives the CFTC authority to regulate swaps. The key legal questions being grappled with bycourts throughout the USare whether event contracts offered by prediction markets qualify as swaps, and whether the CFTC jurisdiction over swaps preempts states from applying their gambling laws.

The CFTC is suing Utah in the same US district court that previously ruled in Utah’s favor.Kalshi sued Utahin February in an attempt to stop the state from bringing an enforcement action against the prediction market.

In August, US District Judge Robert Shelby granted Utah’s motion for summary judgment and denied Kalshi’s motion for a preliminary injunction. Shelbywrote, “[T]he court concludes the federal law relied upon by Kalshi does not preempt Utah’s ability to enforce its anti-gambling laws.”

Shelby determined the text of US law makes it clear that state regulation is not forbidden. US law states that CFTC jurisdiction does not “supersede or limit the jurisdiction conferred on courts of the United States or any State,” and “explicitly provides for State regulation of its gaming laws in all but a few specified cases,” he wrote.

“Congress is aware that some States permit gambling while others do not, and the CEA explicitly provides for State jurisdiction,” Shelby wrote.

Kalshi is now appealing its loss to the US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit but was unable to obtain an injunction preventing enforcement of the state gambling ban while that litigation continues. On September 8, Tenth Circuit judgesdeniedKalshi’s emergency motion for an injunction pending appeal. Utah filed its lawsuit seeking a shutdown of Kalshi about six weeks later.

The CFTC lawsuit against Utah makes arguments similar to the ones already rejected by the district court, although some other courts have ruled otherwise.

“Utah is not the first State that has attempted to invade the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction over swaps,” the CFTC lawsuit said. “Already, several federal courts—including the Third Circuit—have swiftly responded by issuing or affirming temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions barring the States from enforcing their gambling laws against CFTC-regulated exchanges that offer sports-related or other event contracts.”

The Third Circuit appeals courtruledthat New Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets. But Kalshi lost similar cases in theSixth CircuitandNinth Circuitin rulings that went in favor of Ohio, Tennessee, and Nevada.

Because circuit appeals courts are divided on the issue, it is likely that the Supreme Court will take up the case and determine whether states can apply their gambling laws to prediction markets.New Jersey petitioned the Supreme Courtto resolve the circuit split, and 39 other states and the District of Columbia filed abriefsupporting New Jersey’s petition.

item.title: Turning a solar power system into its own backup
item.description:
Plant design allows it to run on either stored solar heat or combustion.

Rather than directly converting photons into electricity, concentrated solar energy uses mirrors to turn sunlight into heat, which can then be used to drive traditional generating turbines. Up to about a decade ago, there was a case to be made that concentrated solar energy had a bright future, as improvements in heat storage had turned it into a way to generate power around the clock.

It wasn’t to be. While concentrated solar costs fell enough to compete with nuclear power, the price of photovoltaics plunged, making solar panels the cheapest source of power in most locations. Currently, if you have a good site to generate solar power, then the economics of PV panels are hard to beat.

That has left us needing to build a mixture of other facilities—typically batteries and natural gas facilities—to handle overnight needs or weather-driven shortfalls. But a small company is promising that it can help avoid the need to build a separate facility. Its version of concentrated solar is designed so that a fossil-fueled backup system shares most of the generating hardware with the solar side.

Concentrated solar, also called solar thermal, is pretty simple in principle. Most of the site is covered with heliostats, devices that incorporate mirrors and a motorized tracking system that can keep their focus on a single point as the Sun moves across the sky. The point of focus is in a tower, where sunlight heats a working fluid. The hot fluid can then be used to power a traditional steam turbine, or its heat can be stored and used to generate power overnight.

There are many potential variations, however: different working fluids and methods of heat storage, trough-shaped mirrors that eliminate the need for a tower, and so on. All of those variants are meant to reduce some of the issues inherent to solar thermal: lots of moving parts, potentially corrosive fluids, and so on. Those issues and the lack of standardization have helped ensure that the costs of these plants haven’t come close to keeping pace with photovoltaics.

Without any incentive to generate renewable power overnight, there hasn’t been any way for concentrated solar to compete. Construction of new plants has largely stopped, and a number of sources have simply stopped tracking the economics of it.

So it was a bit of a surprise to hear that India had contracted with a US-based startupcalled 247Solarto build and operate a small concentrated solar plant. While the plant will be extremely small (1 megawatt) and mix in photovoltaics, the company had a unique angle: The same hardware that is handling the solar thermal output can simply be run using fossil fuels if there is a significant shortfall in renewable generation.

“Our systems are their own backup,” said 247Solar’s Mark von Keszycki. “During times of low solar resource—long duration, bad weather, whatever the case may be—they’re able to burn a variety of fuels.”

To understand how this works, it’s best to step back and understand the entire system being built, which includes details about how the 247Solar team hopes to avoid some of the problems faced by other solar thermal systems and provide a great deal of flexibility in terms of how its systems get put to use.

Like other concentrated solar systems, 247Solar’s will be using a field of heliostats. But the receiver—the hardware that they focus the sunlight on—is distinctive, in that it works with ambient-pressure air. (It’s an updated version of hardware developed by a German company.) Air exits this hardware at approximately 970° C. That air can potentially be used directly for industrial process heat or sent on to the hardware that generates electricity. But in most cases, it will be directed to heat storage.

Rather than dealing with molten salts and potential phase transition, 247Solar heats up ceramic pellets roughly the size of a golf ball. Depending on the details of the storage configuration, von Keszycki says that the heat from the storage could be used to generate power for anywhere from nine to 20 hours after the Sun sets. Hours will obviously be shorter if some of the heat is used to generate power during the day, but 247Solar plans to pair its system with photovoltaic installations for daytime generation.

Wherever the hot air comes from, it will be sent to a heat exchanger. This is designed as a drop-in replacement for a combustion unit on a traditional turbine to heat up compressed air to drive generation. “The heat exchanger does the same job as the combustor did,” 247Solar’s Bruce Anderson told Ars. “It’s in the same place in the turbine assembly as the combustor was: after the compression stage and before the expander.” The initial installation will pair two 200 kW generators; aside from the heat exchanger, everything else is part of a standard off-the-shelf package.

This is the point where the system’s flexibility comes in: It doesn’t care how the air in the exchanger gets heated. So, any of a variety of fuels can be burned to provide the equivalent heat. von Keszycki suggested that adding the capability to the system to burn fossil fuels tacks on less than 10 percent of its total cost.

The air coming out of the heat exchanger is still quite hot, in the neighborhood of 250° C, and von Keszycki called it “a separate usable resource” that could be directed to a variety of applications, including industrial processes and absorption cooling. Again, if intermediate temperatures are needed, it could potentially be mixed with some hot air coming directly from the storage medium, albeit at the cost of generation.

The first installation will be small, with a pair of 200 kW generators, and so will mostly serve to validate the system’s engineering—Anderson said the biggest worries are “unknown unknowns.” But the system is designed to be modular, and the company is already working through the engineering of a 3 megawatt facility that combines multiple units that share a single tower that holds multiple receivers and heat storage.

The installation will also give the company a sense of how the system actually works out financially. On a typical grid, there are few incentives for providing around-the-clock renewable energy. And the cost of ensuring that there is enough generation to back up solar plants is often absorbed by other parties. The ability to generate fossil-fuel-based backup power without having to build a dedicated facility can definitely savesomeonemoney, but markets aren’t always set up so that it’s easy to extract those savings.

So, it’s not surprising that 247Solar has other markets in mind. It’s especially excited about remote mining sites, which typically require diesel to be shipped in, often at considerable expense. The 247Solar system would avoid that expense, while potentially providing process heat that could be useful for some of the ore processing. And powering mining operations without emissions would work well for companies that are required to account for the carbon emissions of their supply chain.

Still, there might be a space for this sort of facility on the grid, if it does successfully avoid the need for dedicated fossil fuel plants that only ever run for a small fraction of the night—provided the price and incentives line up.

]]>

item.title: Trump ignored intel on China’s Nvidia spy to protect company’s stock, report says
item.description:
Spy accused of exploiting Trump ties to Huang, funneling secrets to China.

Donald Trump apparently is so aligned with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—who has become thepresident’s key advisor on AI—that he ignored intelligence indicating that Huang was the target of a “Chinese spy plot,” and did so partly to protect Nvidia’s stock.

The New York Timesspokewith people briefed on US intelligence agencies’ surveillance and granted them anonymity to discuss findings drawn from “classified intelligence.” According to sources, about a year ago, Trump was briefed that “Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access” to Huang. That “someone” was Alice Huang, or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen and former top executive at a Singapore cloud company called Megaspeed.

According to sources, the US had already suspected that Alice Huang—who is not related to Jensen Huang—washelping China evade export controlsto gain access to high-end Nvidia chips through Megaspeed. But it alarmed investigators to discover that she may have used her role at Megaspeed to gain direct access to Jensen Huang. It’s now believed she may have leveraged that closeness to feed China intel not only on one of America’s leading AI companies, but also to influence Trump’s thinking on AI. As Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent noted last month ahead of Trump’s AI talks with China President Xi Jinping, “the president is completely aligned with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia.”

At least partly due to fears that US action against the alleged spying could hobble Nvidia chip sales or disrupt the delicate US-China trade truce, Trump “chose not to do anything with the information,” sources said.

Soon after US scrutiny increased, Alice Huang’s name was removed from Megaspeed corporate documents. At this stage, it’s unclear “how closely she is still connected to Megaspeed,” NYT reported.

Liu Chang, the spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, DC, told NYT that the US accusations against Alice Huang are baseless. He accused the US of pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against China.

It’s not clear which agencies were investigating Alice Huang or what triggered their suspicions, NYT reported. Sources also could not explain what information she may have shared with Beijing.

Nvidia has denied that she would have had access to any trade secrets, but it seems notable that Jensen Huang did not receive a defensive briefing that Americans sometimes get when they’re targets of foreign spying. Some senior officials think it’s unlikely that Jensen Huang would have “remained unaware” of Alice Huang’s alleged intelligence-gathering for the entire duration of their professional relationship, although Trump was told Jensen Huang had no knowledge at the time of his briefing. It seems possible that Jensen Huang got no briefing because US agencies worried that he might tip her off that “she was being watched,” the NYT reported.

Trump’s deep ties with tech leaders have been criticized throughout his administration, butJensen Huang’s influence increasingly stands out. To critics, the political friendship appears to be largely based on growing his business in China. Since cozying up to Trump, the Nvidia CEO has gottenexport controls relaxedand even struck a controversial dealgiving the US a 25 percent cut of some chip salesso he could try to sell more chips in China. Sources told NYT that “some investigations and proposed trade sanctions involving China or Nvidia” have “ground to a halt within the Commerce Department” due to Jensen Huang’s influence.

No one’s sure when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, but NYT found social media photos that predated her role arranging a Megaspeed purchase of $2 billion in chips over the next year. If those chips ended up in China, the US worried they “could help adversaries like China develop new weapons, surveil dissidents, and leap ahead of the United States in AI development,” NYT reported. To US agencies, it’s particularly concerning that Megaspeed may be doing China’s bidding by supplying chips to giant data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia “that appear to remotely serve customers in China,” NYTreportedearlier this month.

Sources told the NYT that US intelligence agencies conducted electronic surveillance of Alice Huang and found that “she was in contact with an American citizen.” Since agencies could not legally surveil the American citizen without a court order, they sought to unmask the citizen by showing a “need for information.”

“In this case, the unmasking process identified Mr. Huang as the US citizen,” NYT reported.

Megaspeed is an Nvidia customer, and Nvidia has independently investigated whether Megaspeed is funneling its chips to China. That investigation concluded that there were no signs of diversion and that Megaspeed has raised no red flags as a customer, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told NYT.

Both Nvidia and Megaspeed insist that the cloud company has Singapore-based owners, but NYT visited the supposed offices and talked to anyone they could find to probe the actual business operations. Among red flags raised, NYT noted that staffers suggested “it’s not clear” what Megaspeed as a company does and confirmed that the Singapore director, James Tan, lives in China and is “never present.” (NYT’s review of corporate ownership documents showed Tan owns the shell company that owns Megaspeed.)

In that story published earlier this month, NYT detailed how Alice Huang was seemingly growing increasingly close to Jensen Huang, citing several photos of them together. That includes a photo at an event where she reportedly bragged, “I bet you guys I can get Jensen here,” and then he arrived in his trademark leather jacket to take whiskey shots.

Rizzo said that it was common for Nvidia’s CEO to attend parties with customers and partners, where he discussed “updates on the market.” One source told NYT that Jensen Huang had always planned to attend that party.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” Rizzo said. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

However, the US government has been investigating Megaspeed since 2024, and they’ve found suspicious boxes of Nvidia equipment that seem to be ready to ship out, rather than installed. Earlier this year, the Department of Justice took over the Commerce Department’s investigation, and Megaspeed remains under scrutiny even though Nvidia’s probes uncovered no evidence the company was helping China dodge export curb violations.

Aaron Bartnick, an assistant director for technology security and governance under the Biden administration, told NYT that Megaspeed raised “many red flags.” Among them are the company’s “ownership claims and possible ties to sanctioned entities,that should have made Nvidia’s executives question whether they should have permitted the company to have access to its AI chips.”

“It’s hard to see a justification for taking that risk,” Bartnick said.

]]>

item.title: Trump declares robot imports a national security threat
item.description:
President orders trade talks on foreign-made factory robots, threatens tariffs.

President Donald Trump has declared the imports of foreign-made factory robots to be a national security threat—ordering new US negotiations with trading partners while holding out the possibility of imposing new tariffs on such robot imports in the future.

Issued on October 28, Trump’spresidential proclamationrepresents heightened government scrutiny of foreign-made industrial robots that could complicate the manufacturing operations of major US corporations that rely on such robots. Those companies include Detroit automakersGeneral Motorsand Ford,electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla, and aerospace and defense giants like Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

Trump’s proclamation describes industrial robots and machinery as being crucial for producing US military weapon systems along with representing a “driving force” behind all critical infrastructure sectors within the US economy. The proclamation cites an investigation under US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick as having found that US imports of such robots “pose[] risks to the United States industrial base and threatens the long-term competitiveness of the United States in a sector that is increasingly vital to national security.”

The Department of Commerce investigation also supposedly found “unique security and safety risks” that may introduce “significant cybersecurity vulnerabilities that can result in severe consequences to the United States.”

Such wording echoes justifications used by Trump’s Federal Communications Commission when itbanned new models of foreign-made robots,such as robotic vacuums, four-legged robot dogs, and humanoid robots, in July 2026. But that FCC action had specifically exempted industrial robot arms and other fixed or stationary robots commonly deployed in automotive factories and logistics warehouses.

Now Trump’s directive for the United States and trading partners “to adjust imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components” aims to strike new agreements on the issue within 180 days of the proclamation’s date. If no agreements have been reached by then, the proclamation warns that the president may take additional actions, like imposing “tariffs, duties, quotas, and fees” on such imports.

Any tariffs or other fees would, of course, be paid by the US companies importing such foreign-made robots. That would likely increase the cost of US manufacturing operations at a time when the United States has become the second largest market in using industrial robots, with theInternational Federation of Roboticsreporting nearly 38,500 new US installations of industrial robots in 2025.

Major US automotive and aerospace companies often buy large robotic arms for factory floor work from the “big four” robotics makers—FANUC, ABB, Yaskawa, and KUKA—that are headquartered in Japan, Switzerland, and Germany. No US company currently offers comparable heavy-duty hardware for large industrial robotic arms, although the foreign robotics makers have been expanding their US engineering and assembly facilities.

Even Amazon, the company that has arguablydeployed more robot workersthan any other in the world, still uses some foreign-made robots, like Japan’s FANUC robotic arms, despite having significantly ramped up its own in-house robot production and developed certain specialized robotic arms.

Trump’s own proclamation acknowledges that US robotics companies do not produce enough industrial robots to “meet national security needs,” and that the United States “relies on foreign imports for most types of robotics and industrial machinery and for their components.”

If Trump eventually slaps tariffs on US imports of foreign-made industrial robots, that would at least fall short of restricting imports outright. Although as Intel recently showed, major US companiescan still get waiversfrom the Trump administration to continue using foreign-made robots even when a nominal ban is in place.

]]>

item.title: Pentagon IG refuses to investigate Starlink/Starshield slowdown in Ukraine
item.description:
Inspector general rejected request from Democratic and Republican senators.

The Pentagon inspector general’s office declined a request from US senators to investigate restrictions recently imposed on the Ukraine military’s use of SpaceX’s satellite network.

Ukraine, which uses SpaceX’s Starlink service and the military version known as Starshield,said earlier this monththat military drones lost satellite connectivity when traveling above 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour). The limit was removed after about 10 days.

Five Democratic and four Republican senators sent anOctober 15 letterto Department of Defense Inspector General Platte Moring, asking for a probe into the reported disruptions of Starlink and Starshield. The letter asked, among other things, “whether any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield services were directed, authorized, or implemented by SpaceX, the Department of Defense, or other US government entities; whether such restrictions were consistent with applicable US government contracts, and what actions, if any, the Department of Defense took in response.”

Platte told the senators in a letter Tuesday that the questions should be directed to the US Air Force and Space Force,according to CNN. “They are better suited to address the matters raised in your letter and to coordinate any Department responses to your questions,” Moring wrote.

A spokesperson for the Pentagon inspector general’s office told Ars today, “The Department of War Office of Inspector General (The DoW OIG) answered recent correspondence from members of Congress regarding Starlink… We carefully considered the congressional request and determined that the matters raised were best addressed by the DOW. Should new information come to light, we may reconsider.”

We asked the Department of Defense whether it plans to investigate and will update this article if it responds.

The satellite problems “were discovered after the administration threatened to withhold intelligence to Kyiv over its strikes on Russian refineries and after President Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel and ease sanctions on Moscow,” CNN wrote.

The letter asking for an inspector general investigation was sent by Senators Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the top democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee; Thom Tillis (R-N.C.); Dick Durbin (D-Ill.); Susan Collins (R-Maine); Jack Reed (D-R.I.); John Cornyn (R-Texas); Chris Coons (D-Del.); Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska); and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.).

“These restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine’s ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure… Starlink and Starshield capabilities are important components of Ukraine’s military communications infrastructure, supporting command and control, unmanned systems, and operational coordination,” senators wrote.

In addition to satellite problems, the letter raised concerns about reports of intelligence-sharing disruptions and asked whether the “reported intelligence-sharing disruptions and Starlink restrictions were connected.” Senators want to know whether “deliberate policy decisions, technical failures, contractor actions, or other causes” were behind the intelligence-sharing and Starlink problems:

We write with grave concern regarding reported disruptions to critical US-supported communications and intelligence-sharing capabilities in Ukraine that have endangered American personnel and potentially compromised Ukraine’s ability to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks. We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which US diplomatic, military, and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids, amid reported disruptions to intelligence-sharing and early-warning capabilities.

Several days after a report thatMusk ordered the slowdown, heaccused Ukraineof violating Starlink terms of service by using it for lethal drone strikes. Musk said that offensive drone strikes must rely instead on Starshield, not Starlink.

Ukraine officials denied Musk’s accusation that it improperly used Starlink and said the speed limit affected their use of Starshield until it was fixed last weekend. “Ukraine’s Defense Ministry told reporters on Oct. 24 that Starshield was working above speeds of 400 kilometers per hour (about 248 miles per hour) again,”according to The Kyiv Independent.

Musk has said that all limits on Starshield speed and usage “are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.” Trump denied ordering the restrictions, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration had “no foreknowledge” of the slowdown.

Shaheen yesterday said, “It is concerning that the inspector general has apparently decided not to investigate satellite communication disruptions that Ukraine relies on to protect its civilians,” according to CNN.

Shaheen said the Trump administration and SpaceX gave “conflicting accounts of what led to those disruptions, which weakened Ukraine’s defenses and put American personnel in Ukraine at risk unnecessarily. There must be an independent accounting and review to determine responsibility and prevent this from happening in the future. I urge the inspector general to conduct a full investigation.”

Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday reportedly called Elon Musk a “genius” while discussing Russia’s plan to build a satellite constellation. Putin made the comment at the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow.

“The admission was all the more striking because a version of Starlink, developed by Musk’s SpaceX, has been used by Ukraine’s military throughout the war with Russia as a key component of drone operations and battlefield communications,”Reuters wrote in an articledescribing Putin’s comments.

Putin reportedly made his comments during a presentation by a Russian government minister who was describing Russia’s initial launches of 30 satellites. “Just a second, ⁠I want to point out this is just our first step. Elon Musk is a genius, he’s just a real genius,” Putin said, according to Reuters.

Putin noted that Starlink already operates thousands of satellites, “while we are only taking our first steps,” and said he has been in “close contact” with Musk.

“We ‌are in ⁠close contact with our American partners—including Mr. Musk—because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin was quoted as saying.

]]>

item.title: Windows 11 gets right-click menu improvements as PC revenue slides
item.description:
The latest update also brings a cloud recovery option for PCs that won’t boot.

Microsoft is beginning the rollout of a Windows 11 preview update that finally addresses a persistent power user complaint with the operating system: the right-click menu that obliterated years of muscle memory on command locations, and hid others behind an additional click. The timing for the release is notable, as the announcement comes alongside Microsoft’s quarterly financial report that saw a continued decline in the business of selling Windows licenses for new PCs.

The preview update,KB5127936, is cumulative for Windows 11 versions 26H2 and 25H2. The update will be a gradual rollout before eventually moving on to a normal rollout for all Windows 11 devices once it reaches general availability. The highlight of the new update should calm annoyed users who have spent years with custom scripts and services in an attempt to shape Windows the way they’d prefer it. Users will get a “customize menu” button that controls what commands appear when they right-click their mouse. Users can toggle built-in commands such as Send To or Create Shortcut on or off, rearrange what appears on the main menu, and control which third-party extensions show up in either the main or submenus. The gripe with the right-click menu had been that Microsoft hid familiar command locations behind a top row of icons while moving other familiar commands under the “Show more options” submenu. Now, Windows users will have the ability to customize the whole thing around their habits.

The new preview also highlights a new Windows feature called Cloud Rebuild, a recovery option that can reinstall Windows 11 directly from the cloud, even when an existing Windows 11 fails to boot. Cloud Rebuild will pull the Windows 11 image and needed system drivers directly from Windows Update. Users will not need a custom recovery image or external media to reinstall Windows. There is an important distinction to note however. Microsoft classified Cloud Rebuild as a recovery option, but it behaves more like a fresh Windows install than a repair, as existing applications and files will not be included. Those worried about data security have the option to sanitize entire system drives prior to reinstalling. For a full list of improvements coming to Windows 11, including changes to Xbox mode and settings, you can view the officialMicrosoft release announcement.

Microsoft’s latest quarterly report, released this week, paints a less encouraging picture of its Windows OEM business. “Windows OEM revenue was below expectations and decreased 27% and 28% in constant currency, driven by the Windows 10 end of support demand in the prior year, inventory drawdowns by OEM and channel partners and weaker PC market demand,” said CFO Amy Hood, according to atranscript of the call. The broader Windows OEM and devices category, which includes Microsoft’s own Surface lineup, fell 22 percent, per the earnings release. Hood went on to state that “we expect these trends to continue through the rest of the fiscal year.”

Recent hardware efforts like theSurface Laptop Ultraand broader RTX Spark platform arrived too late in the quarter to register in the results, and Microsoft forecastfurther dropsbefore any possible boost from new hardware can show in its numbers. The news for Microsoft isn’t negative all around, though, as its Azure platform saw a 48 percent jump, and Microsoft Cloud revenue was also up 30 percent, year over year—now roughly 70 percent of the company’s $92.3 billion total quarterly revenue.
